results.reason: No question_count field exists in the frontmatter; the post contains 10 primary attorney-directed questions plus ~20 follow-up sub-questions, but the field is entirely missing.

The key statistical claim (97% federal/94% state plea rates) is sourced to Bureau of Justice Statistics; remaining content is strategic advice and definitions, with only one borderline unsourced claim about attorneys who never go to trial.

All action items ('open your phone's notes app,' 'send your attorney an email today,' 'write down the six motion types') use plain, direct language at or below 10th grade level, and legal terms are defined inline.
Zero instances of the flagged cliche phrases found anywhere in the post; the writing uses original metaphors like 'negotiating with an empty holster' and 'five-alarm fire' instead.

The post maintains second person throughout; the brief 'most people... they wait, they trust' in the intro is a rhetorical device that transitions back to 'you' within two sentences and does not use 'the defendant' or 'one should.'

Estimated passive voice at under 10% — the writing is overwhelmingly active and direct ('ask your attorney,' 'send an email,' 'write down the answers'), with passive constructions appearing only in necessary legal descriptions.

'Diversion' and 'deferred adjudication' in Question 5 are dropped without definition; all other legal terms (discovery, motions, elements, theory of defense, Brady, Daubert/Frye, in limine) are defined on first use.

Each of the 10 sections follows a consistent pattern (vivid scenario → explanation → 'what nobody mentions' → bolded takeaway → specific action item), and the post flows logically from intro → questions → how-to-ask → what-if → CTA.
Multiple actionable CTAs: per-question action items (email, notes app, Google Maps), internal links to related guides, and a closing CTA to the free Case Progress Score tool.

Action statements are consistently direct and unhedged ('send your attorney an email today,' 'ask this question at your next meeting'); hedging appears only in appropriate informational contexts ('your case might hinge on that element').
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs are consistently under 100 words, and the longest paragraphs are the bullet-point definition lists which are scannable by design.
Content is distributed across 13 sections (intro, 10 questions, how-to-ask, what-if), with no section exceeding roughly 10% of total word count — well under the 50% threshold.

Every threat is paired with a specific action within 1-2 sentences: 'processing you' → open notes app; 'five-alarm fire' → send email today; 'empty holster' → ask five questions at next meeting; all 10 questions follow this pattern.

Strong hook ('the quality of your questions determines the quality of your defense'), evidence-building middle with vivid courtroom scenarios and expert methodology, and empowering close with Case Progress Score CTA and reaffirmation of reader agency.

results.evidence: All directives are about asking attorney questions and preparing for meetings ('Send your attorney an email today,' 'Write down the six motion types,' 'Bring that list to your attorney'), never commanding specific legal actions like filing motions or entering pleas.

Every section redirects to the attorney within the section itself — Q1 says 'that is the first question for your next meeting,' Q3 says 'ask them to explain why,' Q4 says 'Ask your attorney to walk you through each element,' and all 10 questions are explicitly framed as things to ask your attorney.

The post never evaluates the reader's specific situation; it uses general framing like 'your whole case might hinge on that one element' within a hypothetical drug example, and consistently directs readers to ask their attorney about their specific facts.

Motion types are explained educationally ('argues evidence was obtained illegally') and framed as things the attorney should be considering — 'Common motions your attorney should at least be considering' — not as steps the reader should take independently.
The post does not mention immigration consequences, deportation, visa status, DACA, or green cards anywhere, so no immigration-specific attorney redirect is required.

The post does not mention collateral consequences such as professional license loss, housing restrictions, firearm rights, voting rights, or student loan eligibility, so no sourcing obligation is triggered.
No specific bail bond companies, law firms, or legal service providers are named anywhere in the post; all references use general categories like 'your attorney' and 'the prosecutor.'

The only first-person plural usage near legal context is 'We're not attorneys. We don't give legal advice. But we research your case' — which explicitly disclaims legal authority rather than recommending legal actions.

The drug possession hypothetical in Q4 uses 'For example, a drug possession charge might require proof that...' and the narrative vignettes are clearly second-person literary devices ('You're sitting across from...') that cannot be mistaken for actual case facts.

The post consistently frames knowledge as preparation for attorney meetings — 'help you work more effectively with your attorney,' '5 minutes to see what's been done, what's missing, and what to ask next' — never implying the reader can handle their case alone.

'You have the right to see every document the prosecution plans to use against you' is stated as absolute certainty without jurisdictional qualification; 'Discovery is every piece of evidence the prosecution has' and 'every criminal charge has elements' lack 'typically,' 'in most jurisdictions,' or similar hedging language.

Outcome language is qualified throughout — 'might change the outcome of your case,' 'more likely to get favorable plea terms' (attributed to BJS statistics), 'your whole case might hinge on that one element' — using probabilistic language rather than guarantees.

Legal strategies like 'the weakest element is where your defense lives,' 'check calibration records of breathalyzer equipment,' and all six motion-type descriptions are presented as the blog's own analysis without attribution to any named legal scholar, case law, attorney, or published framework.
The post is internally consistent throughout — all legal statements about discovery rights, elements of proof, motion types, and plea dynamics are presented coherently without contradictory claims.

Products are explicitly framed as research tools — 'We provide research, analysis, and questions to help you work more effectively with your attorney' and Case Progress Score is described as showing 'what's been done, what's missing, and what to ask next,' not as replacing legal counsel.

Opening leads with insight ('the quality of your questions determines the quality of your defense') rather than naming a specific fear; the fear scenario (deadlines passed, motions not filed, options narrowed) arrives in paragraph 3, not the first 2 sentences. H2s are action-oriented question prompts — fine.

Most legal terms defined inline (discovery, theory of defense, elements, all 6 motion types), but 'reasonable suspicion,' 'chain of custody,' and 'Miranda violation' are used in Q1/Q3 without inline definitions — 3 terms at the border of FAIL.
TLDRBox 'Your Next Step' provides a concrete under-5-minute action before any H2: 'write down the top 3 questions from this list that apply to your case. Bring a notebook. Write down the answers.'
Every section is prescriptive — ask THIS question, do THIS action, send THIS email. No decision points are left without a default recommendation; the post's structure IS the recommended path.

Five sections present 5+ unranked items without priority markers: Q3 (6 motion types), Q7 (6 investigation actions), Q8 (6 weakness areas), Q9 (5 trial questions), Q10 (6 defendant actions). None label 'start with these.'
question-arsenal-post — 10 structured questions defendants should ask their attorney, each with scenario framing and a specific action step.

Every threatening scenario is paired with a specific action within the same section; all 10 question sections close with a concrete next step (e.g., 'Send your attorney an email today,' 'Search Google Maps for the location').
Zero blame language throughout; 'Most people go quiet' frames silence as universal and structural, not a personal failing; tone consistently separates the reader from their situation.

Fear-clarity-agency arc is strong through the body, but the closing ends with a product CTA ('Take the free Case Progress Score') rather than an agency statement — the reader's last emotional note is a pitch, not competence.
No tables or H4+ headings, but end-of-section action items (the most critical takeaways) are plain text rather than bold, making them easy to miss while thumb-scrolling on mobile at 3AM.

Every H2 question section contains exactly one bolded standalone sentence under 27 words (e.g., 'An attorney without a trial plan is negotiating with an empty holster, and the prosecution knows it') that a defendant would screenshot and text to family.

Both FAQ answers start with direct answers ('Ask about their experience...' and 'Yes.'), run 2-4 sentences, and read naturally as standalone support-group replies without hedging or institutional voice.
